title: Which formulas and shortcuts do you need for case maths, all on one page?
description: Everything for case interview maths on one page: the twenty formulas, five mental maths shortcuts and a six-step routine for staying calm.
hook: You need about twenty formulas, a handful of mental shortcuts and one routine for working out loud, and they all fit on this page. Learn the formulas until you never hesitate, use the shortcuts to keep the arithmetic small, and follow the routine so a slip never turns into a panic. Keep this open while you practise.
body:
In this guide

  • The 20 formulas
  • How the formulas combine: one worked example
  • Six mental maths shortcuts
  • Fractions and percentages worth knowing
  • A routine for working out loud
  • Common mistakes
  • Practice
  • Where to practise next

The 20 formulas

Almost every calculation in a case uses one of these. The right-hand column says when each one shows up. For longer explanations and an example of each, read the 20 formulas explained.

TermFormulaUse it when
ProfitRevenue − CostsEvery profitability case. Revenue = volume × price; costs = fixed + variable
Profit marginProfit ÷ RevenueComparing profitability across years or competitors
MarkupProfit ÷ CostRetail and cost-plus pricing
Contribution marginPrice − Variable cost per unitAny "is one more unit worth it?" question
Break-even volumeFixed costs ÷ Contribution per unitLaunches, price cuts, new sites
PaybackInvestment ÷ Annual net cash gainInvestment and cost-saving cases
ROIAnnual profit ÷ InvestmentComparing projects against a hurdle rate
EBITDARevenue − COGS − Operating costs (before depreciation and amortisation)Valuation and private equity cases
Expected valueSum of (outcome × probability)Uncertain launches, bids, lawsuits
PerpetuityCash flow ÷ r (growing: next year's cash flow ÷ (r − g))Valuing a steady stream of cash
NPV ruleInvest if NPV > 0Any investment decision
CAGR(End ÷ Start)^(1 ÷ years) − 1Market growth over several years
Market shareOur sales ÷ Market salesCompetitive cases. Say whether it is units or value
Price elasticity% change in volume ÷ % change in pricePricing cases
UtilisationActual output ÷ Maximum outputBefore anyone adds capacity
LTVProfit per customer per year × Years retainedSubscription and customer cases
CACSales and marketing spend ÷ New customersGrowth and marketing cases
ChurnCustomers lost ÷ Customers at start of periodAverage lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ churn
Cost-to-revenueEach cost line ÷ Revenue, over timeFinding the cost that is growing fastest
Net working capitalInventory + Receivables − PayablesGrowth cases where cash runs short

How the formulas combine: one worked example

Formulas rarely arrive alone. A typical case strings three or four together, so practise the chain, not just the pieces.

A chain sells 50,000 units a year at $30 each. The variable cost is $18 per unit and fixed costs are $400k a year.

  • Revenue: 50,000 × $30 = $1.5M.
  • Contribution: 50,000 × ($30 − $18) = 50,000 × $12 = $600k.
  • Operating profit: $600k − $400k = $200k.
  • Contribution margin: $12 ÷ $30 = 40%.
  • Operating margin: $200k ÷ $1.5M = 13.3%.
  • Break-even volume: $400k ÷ $12 = 33,333.3, so 33,334 units (always round break-even up).

Now the client asks about a 10% price cut to $27. Variable cost stays at $18, so contribution falls to $9 a unit. Break-even becomes $400k ÷ $9 = 44,444.4, so 44,445 units. A 10% price cut has raised the volume needed just to cover fixed costs by a third. That is the sentence the interviewer wants to hear, not the arithmetic.

Notice which margin answers which question. The 40% contribution margin tells you what one extra sale adds. The 13.3% operating margin tells you how profitable the business is today. Use the wrong one and you will badly understate the value of an extra unit. Operating leverage explains why the two diverge.

Six mental maths shortcuts

1. Big numbers: count the zeros separately

4.5M × $300: multiply 4.5 × 3 = 13.5, then add the zeros (six from the million, two from 300) to get 13.5 × 10⁸ = $1.35B. More in multiplying big numbers.

2. Division: cancel zeros first

$4.5B ÷ 1.5M customers: strike six zeros from each to get 4,500 ÷ 1.5 = $3,000 per customer.

3. Percentages: build from 10%, 5% and 1%

17% of 340: 10% is 34, 5% is 17, 1% is 3.4, so 2% is 6.8. Total 34 + 17 + 6.8 = 57.8. More in percentages in your head.

4. Break-even in one line

Fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost). $3M ÷ ($25 − $10) = 200,000 units. More in break-even volume.

5. Growth over several years

Multiply the growth factors rather than adding percentages. Three years at 10% is 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.331, so +33%, not +30%. More in yearly growth rates.

6. The rule of 72

Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ growth rate in %. At 8% a year, 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years (the exact answer is 9.01). More in the rule of 72.

Fractions and percentages worth knowing

Knowing these by heart turns awkward divisions into multiplications. Dividing by 8 is the same as multiplying by 12.5%.

FractionPercentageFractionPercentage
1/250%1/812.5%
1/333.3%1/911.1%
1/425%1/119.1%
1/520%1/128.3%
1/616.7%1/166.25%
1/714.3%1/205%

Two more facts save time. First, x% of y equals y% of x, so 8% of 25 is the same as 25% of 8, which is 2. Second, a price rise followed by an equal percentage fall leaves you lower than you started: +20% then −20% gives 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% drop.

A routine for working out loud

  1. Say what you will calculate and why, before any numbers. Get a nod on the approach.
  2. Write the numbers down neatly, with units. "$/unit" and "units/year" written next to each figure catch most errors.
  3. Round to friendly numbers and say that you are rounding. "I'll call 252,000 a quarter of a million for a first pass."
  4. Talk through each step. Silence makes the interviewer guess where you are.
  5. Check the answer is the right size. Compare it with something you already know, such as total revenue.
  6. Say what the number means for the client. A number without a so-what is half an answer.

Here is the difference in practice.

Weak: "Um, 50,000 times 12... 600... so 600, then minus 400 is 200."
Strong: "Profit is volume times contribution, minus fixed costs. That's 50,000 times $12, so $600k, minus $400k: $200k, a 13% operating margin. That's thin, so a price cut would hurt. Shall I test how much volume it would need?"

The strong version is barely longer. It states the formula, carries the units, gives a margin for scale and points to the next step. Getting through the maths without mistakes covers this routine in more depth.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing margin and markup. A $20 profit on an $80 cost and $100 price is a 20% margin but a 25% markup. Say the denominator out loud. See margin vs markup.
  • Adding growth rates. Five years at 5% is 1.05⁵ = 1.28, so +28%, not +25%.
  • Dropping a factor of 12 or 1,000. Monthly prices need × 12 for a year. Thousands and millions need converting before you add them.
  • Confusing percentage points with percent. A fee rate falling from 15% to 12% is 3 points, but a 20% relative cut.
  • Rounding away the answer. Rounding 5.5B to 5B is a 9% error. Round inputs gently, and in opposite directions where you can.

Practice

Try each one out loud before you open the answer.

1. A store sells 2.5M items a year at $12 each with a 35% gross margin. What is gross profit?

Show the answer

Revenue is 2.5M × $12 = $30M. Gross profit is 35% of $30M: 10% is $3M, so 30% is $9M, plus 5% is $1.5M. Total $10.5M.

2. Price $75, variable cost $45, fixed costs $1.8M. What is break-even volume?

Show the answer

Contribution is $75 − $45 = $30 a unit. $1.8M ÷ $30 = 60,000 units. Check: 60,000 × $30 = $1.8M.

3. A market grows 12% a year. Roughly how long until it doubles?

Show the answer

72 ÷ 12 = about 6 years. The exact figure is 6.1 years, so the rule is close enough for any case.

4. A business produces $6M of cash a year, forever. At a 5% discount rate, what is it worth?

Show the answer

Perpetuity value = $6M ÷ 0.05 = $120M. Dividing by 0.05 is the same as multiplying by 20.

Where to practise next
